final_task_tree.title: Figure out a training plan for my dog
final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

comments.body:
Done — report attached, tree built. Stayed inside the three things you asked for; no crate training, no nutrition, no gear rabbit holes.

**The short version:**

1. **Hybrid, not either/or.** DIY the pulling — that's mechanical and you can do it. Buy help for the barking, because fear-based and frustration-based reactivity look identical on the leash and need opposite protocols, and guessing wrong costs you weeks. Total spend recommended: **$490**.
2. **Three options, all with verified prices:** HSSV "Top Dogs Level 1" $300 (6 wks online, Tuesdays 6:15pm, next cohort 19 Aug) · D For Dogz "Leash Reactive Foundations" $595 (Sat 9:30am Palo Alto + Wed 6:30pm Zoom) · Stacy's Wag'N'Train $190 one-off consult, or $1,500 / $3,000 packages, best credentials of the three. I ruled out Off Leash K9 and Sit Means Sit — both e-collar, and AVSAB's position is that aversives have no role in behaviour modification, no exceptions.
3. **Four-week plan** is broken out as four subtasks with day-by-day drills and a written advance-criterion for each week. Week 1 is deliberately trigger-free: you're breaking the rehearsal habit before you start counter-conditioning.

**Your next three actions, in order:**
- Register for the HSSV class (19 Aug cohort — book before it fills): dogtraining@hssv.org
- Email stacy@wagntrain.com for the $190 consult, and **ask up front whether the eval can be an evening or weekend** — her site says private coaching is weekdays daytime, which is the one thing that could break this plan. If she can't, use D For Dogz' free 15-min call instead (650-538-3011) and skip the $190.
- Buy the gear (front-clip harness, long line, treat pouch, two tiers of treats, ~$60–110) before Week 1 starts.

**One thing I want to flag:** start the trigger journal in Week 1 even if you do nothing else. Distance, what he did, recovery time, and whether his body language reads fear (stiff, leaning away) or frustration (bouncy, straining toward). Handing that to a trainer is worth more than the first half hour of any consult.

Parent set to **waiting** — everything left is yours: two bookings, one shopping trip, and four weeks of reps.

Housekeeping: if a scoping subtask about writing the plan still shows as open, it's superseded — the plan shipped as the Week 1–4 subtasks plus section 3 of the report. Close it.

report.markdown:
> Rescue border collie mix, 14 months, pulls hard + barks at every dog. South Bay CA, evenings and weekends. Three answers below and nothing else.

---

# 1. Trainer or DIY?

**Hybrid. Do the daily reps yourself, buy about $490 of professional help. Not full DIY, and not a $3,000 package.**

The two problems in the brief are not the same kind of problem:

**The pulling is a DIY problem.** Loose-leash walking is mechanical and well documented. A 14-month collie mix picks it up quickly with 5–10 focused minutes a day. Paying someone $150/hour to teach you "stop when the leash goes tight" is a waste.

**The barking at every dog is not a DIY problem — not until one question is answered.** Two completely different emotions produce identical-looking behaviour on the end of a leash: <cite index="27-1">a fearful dog wants to get away from the thing and uses distance-increasing body language like snarling and growling, whereas a frustrated dog shows distance-decreasing behaviour like playful barking and bounciness — "Hey, you look fun! Come meet me!"</cite> <cite index="27-2">Best Friends is explicit that the first step is working out which one you have, because the answer shapes the behaviour-modification approach you use.</cite> Fear needs counter-conditioning and patience. Frustration needs an outlet plus impulse control, and treating it like fear will get you nowhere for weeks. **One hour with a qualified person to get that call right is the best money in this project.**

Three more reasons not to go it completely alone:

- **14 months is the worst possible age to guess.** Peak adolescence, high arousal, herding-breed motion sensitivity. This is precisely when owners entrench the behaviour by keeping the leash tight and walking past dogs the dog can't cope with.
- **The DIY failure mode is expensive.** Every reactive episode is a rep. Rehearsal makes it stronger, and the threshold distance grows rather than shrinks.
- **The tool most people reach for when DIY stalls is off the table.** <cite index="24-11,24-12">AVSAB's 2021 position statement, drawing on the scientific evidence, says "There is no role for aversive training in behavior modification plans," and there are no exceptions to that standard, even for dogs with aggressive behaviours.</cite> That rules out prong collars, choke chains and e-collars — and it rules out two of the biggest-advertising trainers in the South Bay.

**The honest counter-argument:** no bite history is mentioned, the dog is young, you have real time available, and the core protocol is genuinely learnable from free material. If $490 is not available, full DIY on the plan in section 3 is a defensible choice. Just keep the journal, because without it you're guessing at fear vs frustration.

### What to spend

| Buy | Cost | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Wag'N'Train virtual behavior consult | **$190** | Get fear-vs-frustration diagnosed by someone holding CPDT-KA + CBCC-KA. One hour, no package commitment. |
| HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 | **$300** | Six weeks of reactivity-specific structure and accountability on a weeknight evening while you do the work. |
| **Total** | **$490** | Reassess at week 4 and again at the end of the class. |

**Do not buy yet:** Wag'N'Train's $800 "4-pack" (their own page describes it as for dogs *without* real behaviour-modification needs — wrong product), or the $3,000 package (right content, wrong time — that's your escalation option if the cheap tier stalls).

---

# 2. Three local options, real prices

### HSSV "Top Dogs Level 1 (Reactive Dogs)" — $300 ⭐ best value
Humane Society Silicon Valley, 901 Ames Ave, Milpitas CA 95035 · dogtraining@hssv.org

- <cite index="21-1,21-2">Designed specifically for dogs struggling with leash or barrier reactivity; six weeks, entirely online through Zoom, so the dog learns at home before practising in the real world.</cite>
- <cite index="21-4,21-5">Six-week course, one session per week — first session 90 minutes, then five sessions of 50 minutes; for dogs that bark, lunge or worry but have not caused injury.</cite> Dogs 8 months and older.
- <cite index="21-3">Science-based positive reinforcement: threshold work, impulse control, calm exits and real-life coping skills.</cite>
- **Next cohort: Tuesday 19 August 2026, 6:15pm** — an evening slot, fits your constraint exactly.
- Follow-on: <cite index="21-7,21-8">Top Dogs Level 2 is in-person, with real-time coaching in a controlled group setting on the exercises from Level 1</cite> — also $300, six weeks, requires L1 or instructor approval.
- **Limits:** no 1:1 time, no in-home component, and weeks 1–6 are all screen-based.

### D For Dogz "Leash Reactive Dog Foundations" — $595 ⭐ best if you want in-person
Palo Alto, serves San Jose and the South Bay · 650-538-3011

- <cite index="19-0,19-1,19-2">Tuition $595 for 9 sessions completed in 5 weeks: in-person classroom Saturdays 9:30–10:30 AM, plus live Zoom Q&A and troubleshooting Wednesdays 6:30–7:15 PM.</cite> Both slots fit evenings/weekends.
- <cite index="19-3,19-4">The first two in-person sessions are people-only so you learn the concepts and handling without pressure on the dog, and the final session is a guided neighbourhood walk.</cite>
- Method: positive reinforcement, teaching the dog to disengage from triggers and re-orient to you, with controlled setups at manageable distance and changed associations. Requirements: current vaccinations, no bite history toward humans.
- Graduate programme ("Reactive to Distinguished Dogz"): <cite index="19-8,19-9,19-10,19-11">$500 per month — in-person group sessions in real public settings on the 1st and 3rd Saturdays, Zoom troubleshooting on the 2nd and 4th Wednesdays, plus one 60-minute in-person or two 30-minute virtual private sessions each month, and community access</cite>. Only local option that bundles ongoing 1:1 — but don't commit to that now.
- Private reactive training exists but **price is not published**; there's a free 15-minute discovery call to get a quote.
- They also run free monthly reactive-dog owner support groups, open to non-clients.

### Stacy's Wag'N'Train — $190 / $1,500 / $3,000 ⭐ best credentials
Stacy Braslau-Schneck, MA CPDT-KA CBCC-KA · San Jose since 1998 · stacy@wagntrain.com (email only, no public phone)

- <cite index="26-0">Behaviour Consultation/Evaluation: about an hour, $190, or included in any package.</cite> Delivered over Zoom. **This is the one to buy.**
- <cite index="17-0,17-1">Basic "4-pack" $800 — four one-hour private lessons, described as good for basic training for puppies or new dogs without real behaviour-modification issues.</cite> Not your dog.
- <cite index="17-3,17-4">Beginning Behaviour Modification "6-pack" $1,500 — six one-hour private lessons, virtual or in-person, stated as good for dogs with minor aggression or other serious issues.</cite>
- <cite index="17-6,17-7">Behaviour Modification Foundation $3,000 — 14 one-hour lessons, five weekly then eight biweekly, designed for dogs with aggression, anxiety, fearfulness, leash-reactivity and barking.</cite> The right content if you escalate.
- **⚠️ Scheduling risk:** <cite index="17-9,17-10">private lesson coaching appointments are available on weekdays during the daytime, and due to high demand are often booked 2–3 weeks in advance.</cite> Confirm an evening/weekend slot for the initial virtual eval before counting on her.

### Ruled out
| Provider | Why |
|---|---|
| Off Leash K9 San Jose | E-collar based. Fails the AVSAB standard above. |
| Sit Means Sit Sunnyvale | Same. |
| Dogs in Harmony, Sunnyvale | Reward-based and well reviewed, but publishes no prices and has no reactivity-specific programme. Backup only. |
| Petco / big-box classes | No reactivity track. A reactive dog in a general obedience class is a setup for failure. |

---

# 3. The first four weeks

Two protocols running in parallel: **loose-leash mechanics** (daily, low stakes) and **counter-conditioning to dogs** (3–4 short sessions a week, always under threshold). Every week is broken out as its own subtask with the full detail.

### Rules that start on day one and never stop
- **Never let the leash go tight while he's looking at a dog.** <cite index="27-6,27-7">The leash stops a fearful dog fleeing, so it switches to "fight" instead, and for a frustrated dog it blocks what he wants and adds to the frustration; your own stress also travels down a taut leash, so keep it loose and breathe slowly.</cite>
- **Cross the street or U-turn early, every time.** No head-on passes on narrow pavements.
- **Walk at off-peak hours** for the next month. Fewer dogs = fewer rehearsals.
- **Watch for trigger stacking.** <cite index="27-11,27-12">Lots of small triggers accumulate — each one alone wouldn't tip him over, but piled up they do.</cite> A bad session usually means he was already loaded before you left the house.

### Week 1 — no triggers, no pulling
Rebuild the walk from scratch. Deliberately avoid other dogs; **zero reactive episodes is the win condition.**
- Daily: 5 min marker training indoors (mark, then treat, 20 reps — <cite index="27-16">the marker is a contract: if you use it, you must reward, even accidentally</cite>), then 10 min loose-leash work somewhere empty. Leash slack = you walk. Leash tight = you stop dead or turn around. He never gets forward progress from a tight leash.
- 5 emergency U-turn reps per walk with no dog present, so it's automatic before you need it.
- Weekend: one 45-min long-line decompression sniffing walk somewhere wide open. Not a training session — sniffing lowers arousal.
- **Trigger journal every day.** <cite index="27-9,27-10">Identify the specific triggers — they can be very specific, like men with beards or dogs bigger than yours — and a journal is a useful way to pinpoint them.</cite> Record distance, what he did, recovery time, and whether the body language read fear or frustration. Bring this to the consult.
- **Advance when:** 10 minutes of slack leash in a quiet place, and he turns to you when you mark.

### Week 2 — find the threshold, start Look At That
<cite index="27-8">The threshold is the point at which a trigger produces a behaviour change</cite> — <cite index="27-13">distance is the key factor, though not the only one.</cite> Sit somewhere dogs pass predictably, start 100+ feet out, and close in only until you find the distance where he sees a dog and does *not* react. Write it down. Expect 40–80 feet, i.e. much further than feels reasonable.

Then run LAT, 3–4 sessions, 10 minutes max, always at or beyond that distance: <cite index="28-2,28-3,28-4">start under threshold — the moment he spots the trigger without reacting, mark and treat; he should turn toward you in anticipation, and if he does, repeat 10–15 times. If he doesn't turn to you, either the marker isn't understood in that environment or you're too close, so increase the distance.</cite> <cite index="28-5,28-6">Once he's consistently looking at the trigger without reacting, start marking him giving you eye contact instead.</cite> <cite index="28-9">If he goes over threshold and reacts, just increase the distance with an emergency U-turn until he's no longer upset, then carry on.</cite> No scolding, no yanking.

<cite index="28-14">Don't pet him during this work — you can't reinforce fear by coddling, but it may make him feel more trapped or lead him to redirect onto you.</cite>

**Do not close the distance this week.**

If it turns out to be frustration rather than fear: <cite index="28-16,28-17,28-18">LAT still applies because it teaches a better response, but avoid physically holding him back as that increases frustration and risks a redirection bite</cite> — and <cite index="28-20,28-21">add an appropriate outlet, since a dog who lunges because he wants to play needs somewhere legitimate to do that, alongside a physically and mentally enriching life that lowers his baseline</cite>. Plus impulse control: sit-and-wait at every doorway and kerb.

**Advance when:** 8 of 10 sightings at threshold produce look-then-check-in with no barking.

### Week 3 — shrink the distance, add movement
- <cite index="28-7,28-8">Decrease the distance gradually, a foot at a time, keeping the marker and treats going as long as he doesn't react — and be prepared to go back to marking him looking at the trigger and work up to eye contact again.</cite> Two reactions at a new distance means you go back to the last one that worked.
- **Parallel walking — the highest-value exercise of the month.** Recruit a friend with a calm dog. Walk both in the same direction, wide apart, never face to face, narrowing the gap across several sessions. You control the other dog, which you never do with strangers.
- Add the **1-2-3 pattern game** for ambushes you can't avoid: count aloud while walking, feed on "three", repeat. Gives him a job and keeps him moving past instead of fixating.
- Start fading food on loose-leash walking only. Keep paying generously for dog-sightings.
- **Advance when:** he holds it together with a *moving* dog at roughly half the Week 2 distance.

### Week 4 — generalise, then decide
- Short 10-min sessions in **3–4 new locations** (different neighbourhood, evening car park, outside a dog park, quiet downtown pavement). Dogs don't generalise; reset to a generous distance in each new place.
- One normal evening walk on your usual route with the management rules still on. Count episodes; compare with Week 1.
- Loose leash should now hold for a full 15 minutes on intermittent food, with one added distraction per session.

**End-of-month review, journal in hand:** threshold distance Week 1 vs now (halved or better = it's working); episodes per walk (trending down); recovery time (often improves *before* the barking does). <cite index="28-12">Expect this to be slow — deep-seated fears take a long time to change, and baby steps are still progress.</cite>

| Result | Next move |
|---|---|
| Clearly improving | Carry on solo + finish the HSSV class. Then HSSV Top Dogs Level 2 ($300, in-person) to work around real dogs under supervision. |
| Flat or worse | Escalate: D For Dogz in-person reactive work (650-538-3011) or Wag'N'Train's $3,000 package. Ask your vet about a veterinary behaviorist referral — <cite index="24-14">for more complex behaviour issues it can be necessary to add behaviour modification, extra management, and sometimes medication</cite>. |
| Any bite or near-bite | Stop the plan, get professional help immediately. Don't wait for Week 4. |

subtasks.title: Decide: DIY vs. hire a trainer for leash pulling + dog reactivity
subtasks.description:
RECOMMENDATION: hybrid — DIY the daily work, but buy a small amount of professional help. Do not go full DIY, and do not buy a $3,000 package.

Reasoning:
- The leash pulling on its own is a pure DIY problem. Loose-leash walking is mechanical, well documented, and a 14-month collie mix learns it fast with 5–10 min/day of correct practice.
- The barking at every dog is not. Two different emotions produce identical-looking behaviour: fear (dog wants distance) and frustration (dog wants to greet). Best Friends' guidance is explicit that you determine the cause from body language first because it shapes which protocol you use — fear-based needs counter-conditioning, frustration-based needs an appropriate outlet plus impulse control. Guessing wrong wastes weeks. One hour with a qualified person to get that call right is the highest-value money in this whole project.
- Border collie mix at 14 months = peak adolescence, high arousal, herding-breed sensitivity to motion. This is the age where owners accidentally entrench the behaviour, usually by tightening the leash and pushing past the dog's threshold on every walk.
- Cost of being wrong is high: rehearsed reactivity gets stronger, and the common "fix" people reach for (prong/e-collar) is ruled out — AVSAB's 2021 position statement says there is no role for aversive training in behavior modification plans, with no exception even for dogs showing aggressive behaviour.
- Counter-argument for full DIY: no bite history mentioned, dog is young, owner has evenings and weekends free, and the core protocol (Look At That / threshold work) is genuinely learnable from free material. If money is tight, full DIY is defensible.

SPEND: ~$490 total.
1. $190 — Stacy's Wag'N'Train virtual behavior consultation (1 hr, CPDT-KA + CBCC-KA). Purpose: get fear-vs-frustration diagnosed and the plan tailored. One-off, no package commitment.
2. $300 — HSSV "Top Dogs Level 1", 6 weeks, Tuesday evenings, online, reactivity-specific. Purpose: weekly structure and accountability while the owner does the reps.
Then reassess. If after those six weeks the dog still can't hold it together at 30 feet, escalate to D For Dogz' in-person reactive work rather than adding more online classes.

DO NOT BUY: Wag'N'Train's $800 "4-pack" (explicitly described as for dogs without real behavior-mod needs) or the $3,000 package (right content, wrong time — buy it only if the cheap tier fails).

The 4-week day-by-day plan is in the report on the parent task, and broken out as the Week 1–Week 4 subtasks.

subtasks.title: Write the 4-week week-by-week training plan
subtasks.description: Build a concrete 4-week plan the owner can run in evenings and weekends: loose-leash walking mechanics plus a counter-conditioning protocol for dog reactivity. Each week needs specific daily drills, session lengths, and a success criterion for moving to the next week. Goes in the report.

subtasks.title: Buy the gear before Week 1 starts
subtasks.description:
Needed before day 1:
- Front-clip harness (Y-shaped, e.g. Balance Harness, PetSafe Easy Walk, Ruffwear Front Range) — front clip so pulling turns the dog rather than letting him lean into it. No prong collar, no choke chain, no e-collar (AVSAB 2021: no role for aversive tools in behaviour modification).
- 6 ft flat leash for training + a 15–20 ft long line for decompression sniffing walks.
- Treat pouch that clips to your waist. You cannot do this with treats in a pocket.
- Two tiers of treats: everyday kibble/training treats for loose-leash work, and high-value (string cheese, boiled chicken, hot dog coins) reserved ONLY for dog-sightings. Buy about a week's worth.
- Optional: clicker, if you'd rather not use a verbal marker.
Budget roughly $60–110 total.

Action: register via hssv.org/behavior-management-classes (registration goes through their event links) or email dogtraining@hssv.org to confirm a seat. Humane Society Silicon Valley, 901 Ames Ave, Milpitas CA 95035.

subtasks.title: Book the $190 virtual behavior consult with Stacy's Wag'N'Train
subtasks.description:
$190, ~1 hour, over Zoom. Stacy Braslau-Schneck, MA CPDT-KA CBCC-KA, training in San Jose since 1998. Email stacy@wagntrain.com — email is her stated preferred contact, there is no public phone number.

What to ask her, specifically:
1. Is this fear-based or frustration-based reactivity? (This is the whole point of the consult — it determines which protocol to run.)
2. What is his current threshold distance for another dog, and how should I measure it myself?
3. Given evenings and weekends only, which walk routes/times in my neighbourhood should I be using and which should I stop using?
4. Is the $1,500 six-session behaviour-mod package worth it for this dog, or is the class-plus-homework route enough?

Heads-up on scheduling: her site says private lesson coaching appointments are weekdays during the daytime, and that she's often booked 2–3 weeks out. Confirm in your first email that the initial virtual evaluation can be scheduled in an evening or on a weekend. If it can't, use D For Dogz' free 15-minute discovery call instead (see next task) and skip the $190.

subtasks.title: Fallback: book D For Dogz' free 15-min discovery call
subtasks.description:
Only needed if Wag'N'Train can't do an evening/weekend slot, or if you'd rather go in-person from the start.

D For Dogz (KT / Kaajal Tiwary), Palo Alto, serves San Jose and the South Bay. Phone 650-538-3011. Free 15-minute discovery call bookable from dfordogtraining.com/reactive-dog-training-silicon-valley.

Their "Leash Reactive Dog Foundations" class is $595 for 9 sessions over 5 weeks: Saturdays 9:30–10:30 AM in person plus Wednesdays 6:30–7:15 PM live Zoom Q&A. First two in-person sessions are people-only, final session is a guided neighbourhood walk. Fits evenings/weekends cleanly.

Ask on the call: (1) price for private reactive training, since it isn't published; (2) next Foundations start date; (3) whether the Saturday location works for your commute. Note the graduate programme is $500/month — do not commit to that now.

They also run free monthly reactive-dog owner support groups, open to non-clients. Worth asking about regardless.

subtasks.title: Week 1 — no triggers, no pulling: rebuild the walk from scratch
subtasks.description:
GOAL: stop rehearsing the problem, install the marker, get loose-leash mechanics in low-stakes places. You are deliberately AVOIDING other dogs this week. Zero reactive episodes is the win condition.

Daily (evenings, ~20 min total):
- 5 min marker training indoors: say "yes" (or click), then treat, 20 reps. Then mark any voluntary eye contact. The marker is a promise — if you say it, he gets the food, every time.
- 10 min loose-leash walking in the least busy place you can find (empty cul-de-sac, quiet business park after hours, school lot in the evening). Rule: leash goes slack, you walk. Leash goes tight, you stop dead and wait, or turn and walk the other way. He never gets forward progress from a tight leash. Feed at your left knee every 3–5 steps at first.
- Practise the emergency U-turn 5x per walk with no dog present: cheerful "let's go!", pivot 180°, treat as he catches up. This has to be automatic before you need it.

Weekend (either day, 45 min):
- One long-line decompression walk somewhere open where you can see dogs coming from far off — hills, big fields, wide fire roads. Let him sniff freely on the 15–20 ft line. Sniffing lowers arousal; this is not a training session.

MANAGEMENT RULES that start now and never stop:
- Cross the street, step behind a parked car, or U-turn the moment you see a dog. Never walk him head-on past another dog on a narrow sidewalk.
- Never let the leash go tight while he's looking at a dog. Tension feeds both fear and frustration.
- Walk at off-peak hours (late evening) for the next month.

TRIGGER JOURNAL — keep it every day this week: date/time, what the trigger was (size, breed, on/off leash, moving toward or away), how far away, what he did, how long to recover. Also note whether his body language reads FEAR (stiff, leaning back, hackles, growl, wants distance) or FRUSTRATION (bouncy, whining, tail high and wagging, straining forward, wants to greet). Bring this journal to the behavior consult — it's the single most useful thing you can hand a trainer.

MOVE TO WEEK 2 WHEN: he can walk 10 minutes on a slack leash in a quiet place, and he turns to you when you mark.

subtasks.title: Week 2 — find his threshold and start Look At That at a distance
subtasks.description:
GOAL: work out how far away a dog has to be before he can still think, then start paying him for noticing dogs calmly.

FIND THE THRESHOLD (weekend, 45 min): park yourself somewhere dogs pass predictably but far off — a bench at the edge of a park, the far corner of a plaza. Start absurdly far away, 100+ feet. Move in only until you find the distance where he SEES a dog but does not bark, stiffen or lunge. That distance is your threshold. Write it down. It is your working distance for everything below. For most dogs at this stage it's 40–80 feet — expect it to be much further than you'd like.

LOOK AT THAT (LAT), 3–4 sessions this week, 10 minutes MAX each, always at or beyond threshold:
1. Dog appears. The instant he looks at it and does NOT react, mark and feed.
2. He should swing his head back to you for the food. If he doesn't, you're too close — back up.
3. Repeat 10–15 times per session.
4. When he's reliably looking at the trigger without reacting, start marking the moment he voluntarily looks BACK at you.
5. If he goes over threshold and starts barking: no scolding, no yanking. Emergency U-turn, get distance, let him settle, then either resume further away or end the session.

DO NOT close the distance this week. Distance shrinks in Week 3, not now.

Keep going daily: 10 min loose-leash work, 5 U-turn reps, one long-line sniffing walk on the weekend.

FRUSTRATION VARIANT: if the journal and/or the trainer says frustration rather than fear, keep running LAT but add an outlet — one or two good off-leash play sessions a week with a known, well-matched dog, or a vetted daycare. And add impulse control: sit-and-wait at every doorway and kerb. Never physically hold him back while he strains; that escalates frustration and risks a redirected bite.

MOVE TO WEEK 3 WHEN: at your threshold distance, 8 out of 10 dog-sightings produce look-then-check-in with no barking.

subtasks.title: Week 3 — shrink the distance, add movement
subtasks.description:
GOAL: same behaviour, closer in, and while both dogs are moving.

CLOSE THE GAP: reduce working distance in small increments — a few feet at a time, and only after a clean session at the current distance. If he reacts twice at a new distance, go back to the last distance that worked and stay there for the rest of the week. Progress is not linear; a bad day usually means he was already stressed before you left the house (trigger stacking).

ADD PARALLEL WALKING (best single exercise this week): recruit a friend with a calm, non-reactive dog. Walk both dogs in the same direction, wide apart — across a field or on opposite sides of a wide street — never face to face. Feed your dog for staying loose and checking in. Gradually narrow the gap over multiple sessions. This is far more useful than passing strangers because you control the other dog. Two sessions this week if you can arrange them.

ADD A PATTERN GAME for when a dog appears suddenly and you can't get distance: the 1-2-3 game. Count "one, two, three" out loud while walking, feeding on "three", repeat. The predictable rhythm gives him something to do and keeps him moving past the trigger instead of fixating.

Keep going: LAT sessions 3–4x/week at 10 min, daily loose-leash practice, weekend decompression walk. Start fading treats on loose-leash walking specifically — go from every 3–5 steps to intermittent, unpredictable rewards. Keep paying generously for dog-sightings; do not fade those yet.

MOVE TO WEEK 4 WHEN: he can hold it together with a moving dog at roughly half your Week 2 threshold distance.

subtasks.title: Week 4 — real-world generalisation and the reassess decision
subtasks.description:
GOAL: move the skill out of the practice spots and into actual walks, then decide what happens next.

GENERALISE: run short 10-minute sessions in three or four NEW locations — a different neighbourhood, a shopping-centre car park in the evening, near (not inside) a dog park, a downtown pavement at a quiet hour. Dogs do not generalise; a skill that works on your street is a skill that works on your street. Reset your working distance to something generous in each new place.

PROOF THE WALK: take one normal evening walk on your usual route with the management rules still in force (cross the street, U-turn early, leash stays slack). Count reactive episodes. Compare with the Week 1 journal.

RAISE THE BAR ON LOOSE LEASH: he should now hold a slack leash for a full 15-minute walk with only intermittent food. Add one distraction per session — a squirrel, a jogger, a cat — and pay well for disengaging.

END-OF-MONTH REVIEW (do this on the last day, 30 min with the journal in front of you):
- Threshold distance: Week 1 vs now. Halved or better = the plan is working, keep running Weeks 3–4 content at progressively harder distances for another month.
- Reactive episodes per walk: trending down = good.
- Recovery time after an episode: shorter = good, and this often improves before the barking does.

DECISION POINT:
- Clearly improving → carry on solo, plus finish the HSSV class. Consider HSSV Top Dogs Level 2 ($300, in-person, needs L1) to practise around real dogs under supervision.
- Flat or worse, or you've had episodes you couldn't defuse → escalate. Book D For Dogz in-person reactive work (650-538-3011) or the Wag'N'Train $3,000 behaviour-mod package, and ask your vet about a referral to a veterinary behaviorist. Ongoing anxiety that doesn't respond to good behaviour work sometimes needs medication alongside training, and that's a vet decision.
- Any bite or near-bite at any point → stop the plan and get professional help immediately. Don't wait for Week 4.
